items.stem:
Read the passage below, based on the play 'The Proposal', and answer.

"RAJAT (nervously, wiping his brow): Sir, I have come on a very important matter … I mean, about the boundary of our gardens …
MR SHARMA: The boundary? My dear boy, the mango tree is on our side.
RAJAT: With respect, sir, the mango tree has always been ours.
MR SHARMA (rising): Always? Since when, young man?
(Rajat clutches his chest.) RAJAT: My heart … it is beating so fast …"

What do the words in brackets in the scene tell the reader?
items.answer: They are stage directions describing the actions of the characters.
items.markingKey: They are stage directions describing the actions of the characters. (1–2 marks for a complete answer.)

items.stem: How does Chekhov satirise marriage in the play? Answer in about 40 words.
items.answer: Marriage is treated as a business deal about land and property; both families are more interested in land than love.

items.stem:
Read the passage below, based on the play 'The Proposal', and answer.

"In many old comedies, marriages are arranged not between two people but between two pieces of land. Fathers count fields and cattle, mothers count dowries, and the young couple are the last to be asked. Playwrights have long laughed at such bargains, showing that a quarrel over a boundary can easily outweigh a promise of love."

Answer the following:
(i) In old comedies, marriages were often arranged between …  (a) two schools  (b) two pieces of land  (c) two kingdoms  (d) two cities
(ii) Who were the last to be asked?
(iii) What have playwrights shown about such bargains?
(iv) How does "The Proposal" fit this description?
items.answer: (i) (b) two pieces of land (ii) The young couple. (iii) That a quarrel over a boundary can outweigh a promise of love. (iv) Lomov and Natalya quarrel over the Oxen Meadows and dogs instead of discussing love.
items.markingKey: (i) (b) two pieces of land (ii) The young couple. (iii) That a quarrel over a boundary can outweigh a promise of love. (iv) Lomov and Natalya quarrel over the Oxen Meadows and dogs instead of discussing love. (1 mark each, 4 marks.)
